idiom_name: open/abstract base class (single superclass, final by default)
implementation_notes: Kotlin classes are final by default, so the layer supertype is declared open or abstract; abstract implies open, cannot be instantiated, and may mix abstract members (the layer's requirements) with concrete ones (the shared implementation), while an overriding member stays open unless marked final. Interfaces with default implementations supply shared behavior without spending the single superclass slot and compile to JVM default methods, but they cannot hold state, so a layer that shares fields needs an abstract class. When several supertypes provide the same member Kotlin requires an explicit override and a super<Type>.member() call, keeping the resolution of the layer's contract visible.
pitfalls: Base constructors and init blocks run before subclass state is initialised, so calling an open member there reaches a half-constructed override.
Kotlin refuses implicit resolution when a member is inherited from both a class and an interface, so adding a member to the base can break existing subclasses at compile time.
data classes cannot be open or abstract, so layer members that need value semantics cannot extend the base.
